4K LAND AND CATTLE COMPANY’S APPEAL OF SOAH ORDER NO. 13 DENYING
              MOTIONS FOR ROUTE ADEQUACY HEARING

           4K Land and Cattle Company files this Appeal of SOAH Order No. 13, which denied the
motions of several intervenors challenging route adequacy and requesting a hearing regarding the
same. 1
                                    I.    Introduction and Summary
           4K Land and Cattle Company respectfully requests that the Commission reverse State
Office of Administrative Hearings (“SOAH”) Order No. 13 and reinstate the hearing on route
adequacy in this docket. The record before the Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) already
contains substantial, unrebutted expert evidence—including 4K Land and Cattle Company’s Route
Adequacy Challenge and the Expert Report of James Scott 2—demonstrating genuine disputes of
material fact that Order No. 13 either ignores or resolves in Applicants’ favor without sufficient
consideration.
           Order No. 13 improperly cancels the Route Adequacy Hearing thus preventing a full
evaluation of routing alternatives and limiting the Commission’s choices at the conclusion of this

                    II.     Procedural Background and Standard for Appeal

         This Appeal is filed pursuant to 16 TAC § 22.123 regarding SOAH Order No. 13, Denying
Motions for Route Adequacy Hearing and Canceling Hearing on Route Adequacy, issued May 15,
2026. Under 16 TAC § 22.123(a)(1), appeals are available for any interim order of the presiding
officer that “immediately prejudices a substantial or material right of a party, or materially affects
the course of the hearing, other than evidentiary rulings.” This appeal is timely filed within ten
days of the issuance of Order No. 13 in accordance with 16 TAC § 22.123(a)(2).
         SOAH Order No. 13 materially affects this proceeding. By eliminating a route adequacy
hearing, the order narrows the range of routes the ALJs and Commission may consider and
approve. The Commission’s Preliminary Order specifically identified route adequacy as an issue

                            III.      Legal Standard for Route Adequacy

           Under Texas law, a CCN application must present “an adequate number of reasonably
differentiated routes” to permit a reasoned choice by the ALJ and the Commission. 9 This is not a
mere counting exercise—the routes must be meaningfully diverse in geography and impacts, so
that the statutory routing factors (PURA §37.056(c)(4)(A)–(D)) can be fully weighed. 10 The
Applicants bear the burden of proof to establish that the routes presented in the Application are
adequate. 11 If an application fails this standard, the ALJ is directed to allow amendment and re-
notice, or dismiss the case without prejudice if amendment is not pursued. 12
           The Commission’s implementing rule, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), requires that an
application for a new transmission line address the criteria in PURA § 37.056(c) and further
requires consideration of whether routes parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way for
electric facilities, roads, highways, railroads, or other linear utility rights-of-way; whether routes
parallel property lines or other natural or cultural features; and whether routes conform with the
policy of prudent avoidance.

            The purpose of a preliminary route-adequacy hearing is to perform a more cursory review
of the application to determine whether it contains an adequate justification for the routes selected
and whether additional routes should be added at an early stage in the contested case process. 13
Once an applicant makes a prima facie showing that its application is adequate, according to SOAH
Order No. 13, the parties challenging route adequacy “must present evidence showing the
inadequacy of an application or routes and presenting other superior routes.” 14 The applicants can
then rebut this evidence by offering reasoned justification as to why any proposed alternative
routes should not be included. 15
       A. SOAH Order No. 13 Improperly Denies a Hearing on Disputed Facts
           SOAH Order No. 13 improperly reaches a conclusion on route adequacy without affording
4K Land and Cattle Company and other intervenors the opportunity to present their evidence. The
Commission has an opportunity to remedy this error by granting a hearing on route adequacy, the
ultimate merits of which would be analyzed at hearing.
           SOAH Order No. 13 states that “4K Land and Cattle Company’s concerns about the use of
Texas Parks and Wildlife Department resources and recognized EPRI-GTC industry framework
do not pertain to the adequacy of alternative routes in the Application.16 Therefore, they are not
further addressed in this Order.” 17 This summary dismissal ignores the substance of 4K Land and
Cattle Company’s challenge, which demonstrated that the lack of methodology employed by
Applicants—reliance on aerial reconnaissance and omission of documented analytical processes—
is directly tied to the narrow study area and the resulting lack of geographic diversity in routing
alternatives.

            The EPRI-GTC methodology and TPWD resource considerations are not tangential
issues—they are the analytical tools by which an applicant identifies the territory that statutory
factors recognize as corridor-suitable. Where the methodology is inadequate, the study area that
results is inadequate, and the routes generated within that inadequate study area cannot constitute
a genuinely diverse set of choices. SOAH Order No. 13’s refusal to engage with this argument
constitutes a failure to apply the correct legal standard.
           Further, SOAH Order No. 13 treats as established fact several contested representations by
Applicants concerning the purported infeasibility of corridors north of their filed study area. SOAH
Order No. 13 credits, without evidentiary hearing, Applicants’ claims that proximity to Fort Hood
airspace and incremental construction costs foreclose northern routing options. 18 4K Land and
Cattle Company’s expert analysis calls these representations into serious question. The Fort Hood
Military Reservation’s restricted airspace does not blanket the territory north of the filed study
area, and Applicants have offered no engineering study quantifying the alleged cost differential.
These remain live factual disputes that can only be resolved through the presentation and cross-
examination of witnesses at a hearing.
       B. The Application’s Study Area is Anomalously Narrow
           4K Land and Cattle Company’s Route Adequacy Challenge, supported by the Expert
Report of James Scott, demonstrated through quantitative analysis that the study area is
anomalously narrow by every geometric measure applied.
           The BCE filed study area spans only about 35 miles north-to-south, with widths as narrow
as roughly six miles at the tightest pinch. 19 The same Applicants’ contemporaneous Dinosaur-
Longshore proceeding would have placed the BCE corridor approximately fifty percent wider, and
the Big Hill-Sand Lake corridor nearly three times wider. 20 The Centerline Gravity Index confirms
that Applicants explored substantially less lateral space in BCE than in their own contemporaneous
DLS work—a ratio of 0.67x—with a pronounced southward directional bias that DLS does not

       C. The Application Lacks True Geographic Diversity
           Although 122 routes were filed, they collapse into only a handful of corridor groupings, all
converging through essentially the same central counties, crossing the same river systems in
marginally different places, and approaching Bell County East exclusively from the south and
southwest. 22 No route approaches from a substantially northern direction, nor was any northern
corridor investigated despite the potential to avoid sensitive river basins and densely populated
areas. 23 This is directly analogous to Docket Nos. 32070 and 41606, where self-imposed study-
area limitations were found to improperly restrict the Commission’s routing choices. SOAH Order
No. 13 accepts Applicants’ assertion that geographic and regulatory constraints preclude northern
routing, but that finding was made without a hearing and on the basis of disputed assertions that
4K Land and Cattle Company is prepared to rebut with expert testimony.
       D. Expert Analysis Identifies Legitimate Corridor Territory Outside the Filed Study
           Area
           The Expert Report of James Scott applied a four-factor methodology operationalizing each
of the PURA § 37.056(c)(4) statutory criteria—land character, hydrology, critical ecological
features, and people-places-experiences—through independent suitability analyses. Three of the
four analyses identify legitimate corridor territory predominantly outside Applicants’ filed study
area, with the combined envelopes encompassing territory exceeding 100% of Applicants’ filed
study area and thousands of square miles sitting outside Applicants’ filed boundary. 24

legitimate corridor territory located predominantly north of the filed boundary. That northern
territory carries independent statutory significance through associations with Planned Interstate

       G. Commission Precedent Supports a Hearing
            Commission precedent is clear that where routing alternatives are unduly constrained, a
hearing is warranted. In Docket No. 32070, the Commission reversed an ALJ’s denial of a route-
adequacy hearing, holding that confining alternatives to one endpoint “improperly restricts the
Commission’s ability” to consider superior routes. 30 The Commission stated that “[i]t is the
applicant that has the burden to prove not only that there is a need for a proposed transmission
project and the appropriate routing, but also that it has filed an adequate application. It is not
Commission Staff’s or any intervenor’s obligation to prove that an application is not adequate.” 31

unnecessarily narrow routing circle was “not sufficiently supported by evidence” and required
additional routes to be developed from existing, noticed links. 32 The remedy there—requiring
additional forward-progressing routes from existing links—demonstrates that the Commission has
tools to address inadequacy short of dismissing the application entirely.

approximately 17 miles in open terrain, and produce a cumulative viewshed footprint
compounding beyond what any prior Texas transmission deployment has produced. Once

 I. Introduction

On March 11, 2026, in a Certificate of Convenience and Necessity proceeding
before this same Commission, the same Applicants — Oncor Electric Delivery
Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation, by witnesses Julie
Jones and Casey Petty — filed a sworn response on the record stating that
documented weighted-suitability methodology is neither required by PURA nor
authorized by the Commission’s rules. The Application now before this
Commission asks the Commission to certify a 765-kV transmission corridor
selected by Casey Petty and the same routing professionals on the same
methodological posture. The report below identifies the inadequacies of using the
same methodological posture in this proceeding.


II. Procedural Posture

The Application was filed by Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”)
and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation (“LCRA TSC”) on March 26,
2026, seeking amendment of their respective Certificates of Convenience and
Necessity to construct an approximately 200- to 245-mile, 765-kilovolt
transmission line from the expansion of Oncor’s Bell County East Switch (Bell
County) to a new LCRA TSC Big Hill Substation (Schleicher County). The
Application identifies 1,246 alternative routes considered, of which Applicants
advanced 122 to the filed set. Route 894 — the route Applicants identify as best
meeting the factors of PURA § 37.056 — comprises a stated length of 223.7
miles and a stated cost of $1,680,919,000.

In the course of pre-filing notification, Applicants extended the study area
northward and added preliminary links U1–U9 and V1–V8 to the published link
inventory. Of the 122 filed routes, 24 include at least one U-prefix link and 22
include at least one V-prefix link; together, 29 of the 122 filed routes include at
least one northern-expansion link. None of those 29 routes is advanced by
Applicants as the route best meeting the statutory factors.

The intervention deadline was April 27, 2026. Intervenors are parties of record.
The Commission has scheduled a Route Adequacy hearing for May 18, 2026 and
a merits hearing for June 8–12, 2026.

 Texas Government Code § 2001.141 requires every contested-case order to
contain findings of fact and conclusions of law sufficiently specific to permit
review. The Commission’s substantive obligations under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)
and 16 Texas Administrative Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B) carry threshold
significance: the integrated consideration of the factors is what produces a
defensible certificate, and the record the Commission relies on must support the
findings on each factor a CCN order will state.


III. The Statutory Predicate

A. The Statutory Factors

Texas Utilities Code § 37.056(c)(4) requires the Commission, in evaluating a
proposed transmission route, to consider four categories of factor:

               1. community values;
               2. recreational and park areas;
               3. historical and aesthetic values; and
               4. environmental integrity.

The Commission’s rule implementing this provision, 16 Texas Administrative
Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B), incorporates certain PURA factors into the certification
framework and adds further specific routing considerations — in particular,
whether the routes parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way (electric,
highway, railroad, or other linear utility), whether the routes parallel property
lines or natural or cultural features, and whether the routes conform with the
Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance.

The factors cannot be considered in isolation. They pull in different directions on
any real corridor. Consideration of the factors is the act of integrating them. That
integration is the core of the methodology.

Tabulation is not integration; a 38-column attribute table tells the Commission
what is present on each alternative, not how those presences were weighed.

Two further constraints follow from the same statute. The factors must be
considered against an adequate study area — a geographic frame wide enough
that the alternatives examined represent a defensible opportunity space. And the

 consideration must rest on data sufficient to permit findings — the public
datasets, agency consultations, and process expectations the field has established
for siting decisions of this magnitude.

B. The count of alternatives is not the measure of consideration

An Application that places before the Commission 1,246 alternative routes
considered, with 122 advanced to the filed set, is on its face substantial work. The
number is not in contest. What is in contest is whether the segments those routes
recombined engaged the corridor’s diversity, and whether the geographic frame
within which the segments were generated represented an adequate opportunity
space.

The number of routes an Application produces is a function of how route
segments are combined and recombined. A small number of segments can
generate a very large number of routes. Two hundred routes can be produced
from a segment inventory that, on inspection, traverses a narrow band of the
geographic opportunity space the four statutory factors require consideration of.

The Application identifies aerial reconnaissance — overflight of the study area at

appropriate to the construction and operating reality of a 765-kV transmission
corridor is ground-up, not top-down.

III. The Statutory Predicate


A. The Statutory Factors

Texas Utilities Code § 37.056(c)(4) requires the Commission, in evaluating a
proposed transmission route, to consider four categories of factor:

               1. community values;
               2. recreational and park areas;
               3. historical and aesthetic values; and
               4. environmental integrity.

The Commission's rule implementing this provision, 16 Texas Administrative
Code § 25.101(b)(3)(13), incorporates certain PURA factors into the certification
framework and adds further specific routing considerations - in particular,
whether the routes parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way (electric,
highway, railroad, or other linear utility), whether the routes parallel property
lines or natural or cultural features, and whether the routes conform with the
Commission's policy of prudent avoidance.

The factors cannot be considered in isolation. They pull in different directions on
any real corridor. Consideration of the factors is the act of integrating them. That
integration is the core of the methodology.

Tabulation is not integration; a 38-column attribute table tells the Commission
what is present on each alternative, not how those presences were weighed.

Two further constraints follow from the same statute. The factors must be
considered against an adequate study area - a geographic frame wide enough
that the alternatives examined represent a defensible opportunity space. And the



       PUC Docket No. 59475 · Exhibit A · Expert Report of James Scott · Page 5 of 27
 consideration must rest on data sufficient to permit findings - the public
datasets, agency consultations, and process expectations the field has established
for siting decisions of this magnitude.

B. The count of alternatives is not the measure of consideration

An Application that places before the Commission 1,246 alternative routes
considered, with 122 advanced to the filed set, is on its face substantial work. The
number is not in contest. What is in contest is whether the segments those routes
recombined engaged the corridor's diversity, and whether the geographic frame
within which the segments were generated represented an adequate opportunity
space.

The number of routes an Application produces is a function of how route
segments are combined and recombined. A small number of segments can
generate a very large number of routes. Two hundred routes can be produced
from a segment inventory that, on inspection, traverses a narrow band of the
geographic opportunity space the four statutory factors require consideration of.
The route count tells the Commission how many recombinations of a segment
inventory the consultants chose to enumerate; it does not tell the Commission
whether the segment inventory itself, on the geographic dimensions the statute
identifies, represents an adequate consideration of the corridor.

C. The adequacy of the study area as predicate

The factors must be considered against an adequate geographic frame. A study
area drawn too narrowly forecloses alternatives before they are evaluated and
denies the Commission the opportunity space the statute presupposes. Where the
geographic frame within which alternatives are developed is itself constrained,
the consideration of alternatives within that frame is constrained in proportion.
The adequacy of the study area is the precondition of the adequacy of the
route.

Exhibit EX-GRV (Centerline Gravity Index) operationalizes the question of
alternatives-universe lateral exploration as a comparable scalar. The Centerline

of an alternatives universe's segments from the endpoint-to-endpoint great circle,
expressed as a percentage of centerline length. A lower CGI means an
alternatives universe sits tighter to the straight-line endpoint connection and
explores less lateral space. The metric is computed from the segment geometries
Applicants filed; it does not require any external assumption.

The BCE alternatives universe exhibits a Centerline Gravity Index of
3.37%. The Dinosaur-Longshore alternatives universe filed by the same
Applicants on a comparable Texas 765-kV corridor exhibits a CGI of 5.02%.
The ratio is 0.67x: DLS alternatives explored approximately fifty percent more
lateral space than BCE alternatives.

same routing professionals, drawing on the same public-data inventory, produced
an alternatives universe one and one-half times the lateral exploration of the BCE

The constraint is also directional. By length-weighted share, 65.2% of the BCE

BCE universe has a length-weighted signed offset of -2.66 miles south of the

A. Item 266 - Docket 59182 (Big Hill-Sand Lake)

The Application's filed materials describe the route-development process as
iterative consultant judgment. The Routing Memorandum (Attachment 11) does
not document an integrated analytical workflow integrating the statutory factors.
The per-route Environmental Data tabulation reports factor inputs without
documenting their integration. The Direct Testimony of Ms. Petty and
Mr. Marusak explains the process in narrative without citing documented
analytical workflow. The record contains no methodology.




      PUC Docket No. 59475 · Exhibit A · Expert Report of James Scott · Page 17 of 27
 The absence is established by Applicants on their own filing. It is independently
confirmed by Applicants' sworn testimony before this same Commission in
Docket 59182, dated March 11, 2026, in response to a Request for Information
by intervenor Lucius Shipp advancing the analytical critique previously filed in
this docket through FOSS in February 2026 (Items 4):

      "Neither the Public Utility Regulatory Act ('PURA') nor the Commission's rules
      require the type of quantitative suitability modeling described by Mr. Shipp....
      Neither PURA nor the Commission's rules assign weights or values to each
      routing factor or authorize an applicant to do so. Weighted values would
      necessarily be subject to the opinion of the applicant and/or consultant on any
      given project and could be used to make any a 'preferred route. "'

(Docket 59182, Item 266, Admission 1, at 4-5; sponsoring witnesses Julie Jones
and Casey Petty.)

The admission has three features that bear on the Commission's substantive
evaluation. It is sworn - verified testimony o f Applicants' identified witnesses,
not attorney argument. It is Applicants' considered position - offered not as a
concession but as an affirmative defense explaining why documented weighting
is not required of them. And the witnesses sponsoring it in Docket 59182 are the
same routing professionals advancing the BCE filing in this docket. The Direct
Testimony of Ms. Petty in this docket does not contradict the admission. The
Direct Testimony of Mr. Marusak in this docket does not contradict it. The
Routing Memorandum filed as Attachment 11 does not contradict it. By
Applicants' own sworn admission, applied in this proceeding by the same routing
professionals, Applicants disclaim performing the documented weighting that
integrated consideration of the PURA factors would require.

The selection of one route over alternatives nevertheless required relative
valuations among competing factors - that is what selection means. A choice
among competing routes - routes that trade residential proximity against habitat,
cost against community values, constructability against aesthetic integrity - is
an act of valuation. The alternative to valuation is not neutrality; it is arbitrary
selection, which the statute does not authorize. The valuations were performed
somewhere; the admission is that they were not performed on the record.




      PUC Docket No. 59475 · Exhibit A · Expert Report of James Scott · Page 18 of 27
 The only question the Commission therefore confronts is not whether valuations
were made but how - and specifically, whether they are documented (visible ,
auditable, reviewable, sensitivity-testable, comparable across alternatives) or
undocumented ( invisible , asserted , unreviewable ). The Item 266 admission
chooses undocumented. Applicants' representation that weighted values "could
be used to make any a 'preferred route"' is a defense that turns on opacity. The
defense implies - and the record confirms - that the valuations were performed
off the record, inside the "holistic" exercise of consultant judgment whose
reasoning is not before the Commission. Opacity cannot be audited.

This is not an escape from the problem of weighting. It is a concession that the
weighting was decisive and that the weighting was concealed. The admission
self-disqualifies the methodological posture under PURA § 37.056(c)(4). Either
the route reflects decisive valuations Applicants applied but did not document -
a failure of disclosure - or it reflects decisive valuations Applicants declined to
apply at all - a failure ofpredicate. The record contains no third option.

 C. Aerial reconnaissance as principal analytical method

The Application identifies aerial reconnaissance - overflight of the study area at
altitude - as Applicants' principal field method for the BCE corridor,
supplemented by aerial imagery as a GIS base layer. Aerial reconnaissance has
legitimate complementary uses in transmission siting . As a principal analytical
method for a 765-kV corridor evaluated against the four PURA § 37.056(c)(4)
factors, it is structurally inadequate.

Towers are sited on the ground. Rights-of-way are maintained on the ground.
Access - for construction, inspection, vegetation management, emergency
response, and decommissioning - happens on the ground. The analysis
appropriate to the construction and operating reality of a 765-kV transmission
corridor is ground-up, not top-down.

At survey altitude, the landscape compresses. Topographic relief and viewshed
structure flatten. Karst features, springs, sinkholes, and recharge expression are
invisible from above - features whose absence from the analytical record is
acutely consequential on the Edwards Plateau and its margins. Vegetation
community classification at the level the TPWD Ecological Mapping System
requires depends on ground-level signature interpretation that aerial
reconnaissance does not produce. Cultural and archaeological surface features are
not reliably identifiable from altitude. Property boundaries, subdivision plats, and
planned development do not resolve. Trail systems, public access points, and
recreational facilities reduce to undifferentiated patches of cover. Each of those
losses corresponds to a § 37.056(c)(4) factor: environmental integrity under (D),
historical and aesthetic values under (C), community values under (A),
recreational and park areas under (B). The factors aerial reconnaissance cannot
resolve are precisely the factors the statute requires the Commission to consider.

The pattern of layers visible in the filing (residential parcels, hydrography,
parkland boundaries, existing infrastructure - layers identifiable from altitude)
and the pattern of layers absent from it (vegetation classification, viewshed
structure, ecological connectivity, karst expression, cultural-landscape integrity
- layers requiring ground-level data and agency consultation) is the diagnostic
signature of aerial reconnaissance as the principal method.

VIII. Feasibility - The Achievable Baseline

The inadequacies this report identifies cannot be defended on grounds that the
analytical rigor invoked in § § IV-VII is exotic, expensive, or unavailable to a
contemporary 765-kV transmission applicant. The methodology is the industry's
own published standard - EPRI Report 1013080, prepared by the Electric
Power Research Institute and Georgia Transmission Corporation as the industry's
research and operating institutions, and updated in 2019 as Report 3002017601.
The standard's analytical commitments are explicit and on the public record:
documented      weighting,     sensitivity   testing  across   configurations,
multidisciplinary integration of engineering, environmental, community-value,
and aesthetic perspectives, and active public engagement and the integration of
alternative perspectives as part of the analytical workflow itself.

The data is public - drawn from TPWD, USGS, NRCS, NHD, TWDB, USFWS,
FEMA, and the related state and federal inventories accessible to any
transmission applicant in Texas. The analytical capability is established - the
framework presented in § V is one current expression of the tradition the EPRI-
GTC standard codifies.

The same Applicants demonstrated, on a contemporaneous Texas 765-kV
corridor - Dinosaur-Longshore, Docket 59315 - that materially wider
geometric exploration of the corridor opportunity space is achievable using the
same routing professionals, the same applicable law, and the same public-data
inventory. Whether DLS itself meets the methodological standard this report
identifies is a question for that proceeding; what the comparator establishes here
is that the present filing does not meet even the geometric baseline the same
Applicants demonstrated in their own contemporaneous practice.




      PUC Docket No. 59475 · Exhibit A · Expert Report of James Scott · Page 24 of 27
 The Dinosaur-Longshore comparator does not require the Commission to import
that proceeding's findings into this one. It requires only that the Commission take
notice of the achievable baseline Applicants have themselves established -
measured, in the alternatives-universe lateral exploration dimension, at one and
one-half times the rigor BCE delivered - and decline to ratify a filing that falls
so substantially below it.



IX. Conclusion

The visible record reveals a study area drawn anomalously narrow against
documented     Texas    765-kV      planning    practice;    an    alternatives   universe
constrained, by length-weighted measure, to two-thirds the lateral exploration of
the same Applicants' contemporaneous work in Dinosaur-Longshore; a route
situated at the most centerline-pulled portion of an already-tight inventory; and
analytical territory worthy of consideration under the statute's factors that sits
outside the boundaries of the study area Applicants filed. The route inventory's
methodology is, by Applicants' own sworn admission in a parallel proceeding
before this same Commission, not a methodology that performed documented
integration of the statutory factors at all.

What Applicants ask the Commission to do is to certify a 765-kV transmission
corridor selected without the methodology, the study-area rigor, the agency
consultations, the data engagement, and the field practice the statute presupposes.
The Commission should decline to do so on the present record.
